Dechow, Hutton, Meulbroek and Sloan (2001), Short-sellers, fundamental analysis, and stock returns

entries.title: Financial health: F-Score and Z-Score
entries.definition: Two established checks on a company's accounts: the Piotroski F-Score (is the business getting stronger?) and the Altman Z-Score (is it at risk of financial distress?).
entries.hover: F-Score: how many of 9 signs of strength the latest annual reports show (7 to 9 Strong, 4 to 6 Middling, 0 to 3 Weak). Z-Score: five balance-sheet ratios in one figure (above 2.99 Safe, 1.81 to 2.99 Grey, below 1.81 Distress).
body: Where it shows: the Financial health card on each company's page, worked out each night from the latest two or three annual reports.

The F-Score (Piotroski, 2000) gives one point for each of nine signs of strength. Profit: the company made a profit, cash came in from operations, its return on assets improved, and its profit was backed by cash. Funding: debt fell against assets, its short-term position (current assets against current liabilities) improved, and it issued no new shares. Efficiency: its gross margin improved and it made more sales per dollar of assets. 7 to 9 is Strong, 4 to 6 Middling and 0 to 3 Weak.

A check Sift has no data for neither passes nor fails: the card says how many of the nine it could make, and shows Not enough data yet under six. The extra statement lines (current assets and liabilities, gross profit, retained earnings, shares on issue) fill in as each company's statements refresh each week.

Piotroski found that, among cheap shares, those scoring high went on to do much better than those scoring low. It's a quality check that suits Sift's value approach: a share can look cheap because the business is getting weaker.

The Z-Score (Altman, 1968) combines working capital, retained earnings, earnings before interest and tax, and sales (each against total assets) with the market value of the shares against total liabilities. Above 2.99 is the safe zone, 1.81 to 2.99 the grey zone and below 1.81 the distress zone. In Altman's study, companies scoring this low often failed within two years.

What a distress score does: Sift adds a caution to the action's reason ("possible financial distress"). It never changes the action itself, so a BUY stays a BUY: read the balance sheet and the latest results before relying on it.
Banks, insurers and property trusts get no score: both measures were built for ordinary trading companies, and those balance sheets work differently (a bank's deposits are liabilities, for example).

The limits: both were built on United States companies decades ago. The Z-Score was designed for manufacturers, so a fast-growing company that doesn't yet keep profits (low retained earnings) can score low without being in trouble. Treat them as prompts for your own research, not advice.

links.text: Piotroski (2000), Value investing: the use of historical financial statement information to separate winners from losers (SSRN)
Altman (1968), Financial ratios, discriminant analysis and the prediction of corporate bankruptcy (Journal of Finance)

entries.title: Volume
entries.definition: The number of a company's shares that changed hands on the day.
entries.hover: Shares traded each day. The line is the 3-month average; a darker bar traded more than twice that average.
body: On each company's page, below the 12-month price chart: daily volume as bars, with a 3-month average line. Hover a day for the volume and how it compares with the average; the chart's data table lists them.

Why it matters: a price move on heavy volume carries more weight than one on light volume, since many shares changed hands at the new price. Days with more than twice the usual volume are drawn darker: often results, news or a large holder buying or selling.
Small companies trade little, so a few large trades can move their price; that's a reason for care with thinly traded shares.
Volume comes with each night's prices from Yahoo Finance and covers trading on the ASX.

entries.title: Market depth (buyers and sellers waiting)
entries.definition: The live list of orders waiting to buy (bids) and sell (offers) a share at each price.
body: Sift doesn't show market depth. It's real-time ASX data under licence, so there's no free source Sift can use, and it changes every second during trading and empties after the close, so the nightly snapshot Sift works from would tell you nothing.

Where to see it: your broker's website or app shows depth and course of sales (each trade as it happens) to its clients, often free for ASX shares. Look there before placing an order, especially in thinly traded shares.
In Sift, the volume chart (shares traded each day) and short selling (shares sold short) show buying and selling pressure over weeks and months.

entries.title: Is each rule working?
entries.definition: Whether an action's calls beat (or trailed) the average screened share by more than luck would explain.
entries.hover: Sift's verdict on each action: Beating the average or Trailing the average when the difference is very unlikely to be luck, Too early to tell when it could be, Needs more calls under 30.
body: On the Track record page, each action (BUY, INVESTIGATE, WATCH and so on) gets a verdict, a sentence and a bar. The sentence says how far its calls beat or trailed the average screened share and how likely that is to be luck, for example "about a 1 in 40 chance".

The bar shows where the action's true edge most likely sits against the average share (the line marked Average). If the whole bar is to the right, the action is Beating the average; wholly to the left, Trailing the average. A bar across the line means Too early to tell: the difference could be luck.

A tick (✓) means the result is what the action intends: BUY, INVESTIGATE and ACCUMULATE should beat the average, AVOID and SELL should trail it. A cross (✕) means the opposite. WATCH, HOLD, REVIEW and IGNORE are neither.

Sift needs 30 calls before it judges an action. Calls a month apart overlap when the period is longer than a month (two 6-month periods a month apart share five months), so Sift widens the bar to allow for that: it claims less, not more.

Many tests at once. Sift tests every action at every period together, and with that many tests a few would look real by luck alone. It corrects for this with the Benjamini-Hochberg method: a result only counts if it would still stand with no more than 1 in 20 of Sift's findings expected to be luck. The luck odds are the corrected ones, and the bars are widened to match, so a bar clear of the average always means a finding.

It's worked out from each company's first call of each month, the same calls as the rest of the page, and covers the whole history (the monthly summary keeps what it needs after the daily detail is deleted).

entries.title: Chance of reaching a price
labels: Chance of reaching it within 12 months
entries.definition: How often a share whose price moves like this one's touches a level at least once within 12 months.
entries.hover: How often a price moving like this one's touches the level within 12 months, as a number in 10. Based on past price moves only; it doesn't know about news or results.
body: On each company's page, under Price against estimated value: the chance of the price reaching Sift's estimated value and the analysts' target within 12 months, as ten dots and a number in 10 ("Possible: about 4 in 10").

The same words mean the same chance everywhere in Sift: Very unlikely (less than 1 in 10), Unlikely (1 to 2 in 10), Possible (3 to 4 in 10), About even (5 in 10), Likely (6 to 7 in 10), Very likely (8 or more in 10).

How it's worked out: Sift measures how much the price usually moves in a year (its volatility, from up to three years of prices) and works out how often a price moving like that touches the level at least once within a year, assuming no trend either way. A level at or below today's price is already reached.

What it doesn't know: news, results, dividends, or whether the share is cheap. A share far below its estimated value can stay there; a nearby level is reached more often simply because it's close. Treat it as a guide to how far the level is, given how much the price moves, not a forecast.
It's recalculated each night (the Statistics step) and needs about a year of prices.

entries.title: Likely price range
labels: Likely range for the year ahead (two years in three)
entries.definition: Where a share's price would end in a typical year, two years in three, given how much it usually moves.
entries.hover: Where the price would end in a typical year, two years in three, given how much it usually moves. A guide to how much it moves, not a forecast.
body: On each company's page, the share price chart continues past today with a shaded range for the next 12 months, and a sentence above it: "In a typical year, the price would end between $3.05 and $5.78 (two years in three)". Hover the shaded area for the range at each month.
The range widens with time, because the further ahead you look the less certain it is. One year in six the price would end above it, and one year in six below it.

It comes from the share's volatility (how much its price has moved over up to three years) and assumes no trend either way, so its middle is today's price. It doesn't know about results, dividends or news.
Use it to judge how much a share moves, for example how far a fall of 20% would be from normal, not to predict where it will go.

entries.title: Volatility and beta
entries.definition: Volatility is how much a share's price usually moves in a year; beta is how much it tends to move when the market moves.
entries.hover: Volatility: how much the price usually moves in a year (32% means a typical year's move is about a third). Beta: how much it moves with the market (1.2 means about 12% when the ASX 200 moves 10%).
body: Volatility is the typical size of a share's price moves over a year, from up to three years of daily prices. A volatility of 32% means that in about two years in three the price ends within about a third of where it started. It drives the likely price range and the chance of reaching a price.

Beta is how much a share tends to move when the market does, measured from weekly prices against an ASX 200 fund (IOZ, or STW, A200 or VAS). A beta of 1 moves with the market; 1.5 moves about half as much again; 0.5 about half as much; near 0, not much in step with it at all.
Sift recalculates both each night. Beta will drive the crash test simulator still to come: how a portfolio might fare if the market fell sharply.
Both describe the past and need about a year of prices.

entries.title: The theory behind Sift's statistics
entries.definition: The established methods behind Sift's rule verdicts, chances and likely ranges, with the work each comes from.
entries.hover: The methods behind Sift's statistics and where they come from: the t-test, the random walk, beta and the CAPM, and how chances are put into words.
body: Is each rule working? Sift compares each call's return with the average screened share's over the same period, the excess-return method of event studies (Fama, Fisher, Jensen and Roll, 1969, International Economic Review 10(1): 1 to 21). Whether the average difference is more than luck is Student's t-test (Student, 1908, "The probable error of a mean", Biometrika 6(1): 1 to 25), at 95%.

Overlapping calls. Returns measured over the same months aren't independent, which makes a result look surer than it is (Hansen and Hodrick, 1980, Journal of Political Economy 88(5): 829 to 853; Newey and West, 1987, Econometrica 55(3): 703 to 708). Sift widens its error by the square root of the months: simpler than their corrections, and on the cautious side.

Many tests at once. Testing every action at every period means some would pass by chance. Sift controls the false discovery rate, the expected share of its findings that are luck, at 5% (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B 57(1): 289 to 300), and widens every bar to the matching level (Benjamini and Yekutieli, 2005, Journal of the American Statistical Association 100(469): 71 to 81), so the bars and the verdicts always agree.

Volatility and the likely range. Prices are treated as a random walk in the log price, the model behind option pricing (Black and Scholes, 1973, Journal of Political Economy 81(3): 637 to 654; Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, Pearson, on estimating volatility from history). Daily volatility is scaled to a year by the square root of 252 trading days; one volatility either side covers about two years in three.

Chance of reaching a price. How often a random walk touches a level within a time is the first-passage probability from the reflection principle (for example Shreve, Stochastic Calculus for Finance II, Springer, 2004, section 3.7): twice the chance of ending beyond the level.

Beta. How much a share moves with the market comes from the Capital Asset Pricing Model (Sharpe, 1964, Journal of Finance 19(3): 425 to 442). Thinly traded shares understate it on daily data (Scholes and Williams, 1977, Journal of Financial Economics 5(3): 309 to 327; Dimson, 1979, Journal of Financial Economics 7(2): 197 to 226), so Sift uses weekly returns.

The limits. Real prices have more extreme days than the random walk allows, "fat tails" (Mandelbrot, 1963, Journal of Business 36(4): 394 to 419), so ranges are a guide, not a bound, especially in a crash.

Chances in words. People judge "4 in 10" more accurately than "40%" (Gigerenzer and Hoffrage, 1995, "How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: Frequency formats", Psychological Review 102(4): 684 to 704), so Sift leads with numbers in 10 and one fixed set of words.

What's fixed and what's a setting: the calls needed before a rule is judged and the years of price history are settings (Admin, Model and rules, Statistics); the methods above are fixed, so no one can adjust them until a rule looks better.
